english: Romans distinguish living vs dead faith as we do: idle assent vs faith working through love.
Dead faith: believe God; living: believe in God—with love and trust.

title: Only living/formed faith justifies; Stapleton, Bellarmine, Vasquez, Becanus
english: Rome agrees: only living faith that works through love justifies; dead faith profits nothing.
Stapleton, Bellarmine, Vasquez, Becanus: formed faith (with charity) alone justifies.

title: Justifying faith believes in God: trust, hope of pardon, and love (Trent sess. 6)
english: Justifying faith is believing in God: trust and hope of pardon, from which love arises.
Trent sess. 6 ch. 6: grace-stirred disposition toward righteousness through faith, fear, hope, love.

title: Faith not meritorious cause; first justification mere grace (Trent sess. 6 ch. 8)
english: Rome: faith is not the meritorious cause; passage into grace is mere gift through Christ alone.
Trent: nothing preceding justification—faith or works—merits justifying grace.

title: Pontifical dispute: does faith merit justification de congruo?
english: Rome divided: Stapleton—faith merits neither de condigno nor de congruo.
Bellarmine/Vasquez—Trent bars only condign merit; congruous merit of faith allowed.

title: Condign vs congruous merit: all grant free gift; some call living faith congruous
english: Condign = wage from justice; congruous = fitting gift from goodness—no debt.
All Rome: first justification is free gift; 'congruous merit of faith' only means living faith fittingly obtains pardon.

title: Faith justifies as disposition (act) or as part of formal cause (habit)
english: Rome: faith-as-act disposes for justification; faith-as-habit is part of infused righteousness.
Their 'justification' includes forgiveness and interior renovation (sanctification).

title: Not faith alone as opposed to other virtues; other acts also dispose
english: Rome denies faith alone if opposed to other virtues: fear, hatred of sin, hope, resolve, love also dispose.
Infused righteousness = faith + hope + charity habits, not faith alone.

title: Infused virtues real righteousness, yet cannot stand strict divine judgment
english: Infused faith-hope-charity is real righteousness in God's sight—yet cannot stand strict judgment without mercy.
Even the perfect must pray Ps 143:2; last-day reward is of gospel promise, not bare legal standing.

title: Penitent acts are moral conditions, not physical causes of first grace
english: Penitent acts with faith are moral conditions God requires—not physical causes that produce first grace.
Rome (mostly): remission and renovation remain mere gifts; a minority still speaks of congruous merit.

title: First justification free; second (growth) from condign merit of works
english: Rome: first justification (sinner to justustust) is free gift.
Second justification (growth) they ground in condign merit of good works.

title: Nine heads where Roman and Reformed schools commonly agree
english: Nine shared heads: living vs dead faith; only living justifies; repentant conditions; free gift of remission/renovation; fitting mercy to penitents; virtues beyond faith-habit; growth by good works; true Spirit-wrought righteousness God will vindicate; yet none stands strict judgment without mercy.

title: Dispute remains how faith justifies: disposition/form vs Reformed sense
english: Still disputed: Rome—faith as disposing act and part of infused form; Reformed reject that framing.
Once Rome's broad 'justification' (=forgiveness+renovation) is heard, much of their sense is not alien to Reformed doctrine.

title: Reformed deny faith as disposing/formal cause of forensic absolution
english: Reformed: justify = forensic absolution; faith neither merits nor is the righteousness that absolves—Christ's obedience alone is.
Faith is the necessary condition; this need not clash with Rome once senses are sorted.

title: Sola fide: not legal perfection, free pardon; Rome can admit this sense
english: Reformed sola fide: not legal-covenant perfection, but living faith; pardon free, no inherent justice that stands strict judgment.
Rome can easily admit this sense of the exclusion of works.

title: Rome's 'justified by works too': moral conditions + infused virtues God will crown
english: Rome's 'works justify' = repentant moral conditions before grace, plus infused virtues God will crown.
Reformed already concede both; so far the fight looks verbal.

title: Congruous merit of penitential works: private opinion, not common Rome
english: Congruous merit of penitential works is a private Pontifical opinion, not common Roman doctrine.
Even they mean fitting divine goodness—not a justice-debt; Reformed grant the fittingness, reject the word 'merit'.

title: Rome: works condignly merit second justification; Reformed deny 'merit' vs grace
english: Rome unanimously: works condignly merit 'second justification' (growth in grace).
Reformed admit growth by good works under Christ's promise, but deny 'merit'—grace and debt conflict (Rom 4; 11).

title: On these questions: common Rome and Reformed often agree in substance; caveats
english: On these precise heads, common Rome and Reformed often agree in substance despite disagreements over words.s over words.s over words.
Caveats: private oddities; other Roman loci may still undercut this truth; even sound disputants need a benign reading.

title: Roman calumny: Protestants deny inherent righteousness
english: Roman doctors charge Protestants with denying all internal inherent righteousness and Spirit-wrought renovation.
Bellarmine and Becanus pin on Calvin: only Christ's external justice imputed, nothing infused.

title: Campion and Duraeus amplify the calumny
english: Campion: even the regenerate are mere corruption within; grace is only God's favor outside us.
Duraeus: Calvin denies interior renovation even of the blessed.

title: Plan: briefly treat Spirit-wrought inherent righteousness
english: To rebut the calumny, briefly treat the Spirit's justice and holiness in the believing soul.
State what and how much the Reformed ascribe to it.

title: Reformed confessions affirm infused renovation
english: Reformed consensus: God inwardly renews and sanctifies those he receives, infusing new justice imaging Creator and Redeemer.
Polish 1645, Anglican sanctification article, and French Confession all teach living faith with inward vivification and growth in holiness.

title: Fallen man wholly infected outside grace
english: Outside grace man is wholly sin-infected, averted from God, faculties prone to evil.
Original stain darkens mind, warps will, disorders affections—Rom 8:8: the fleshly cannot please God.

title: God heals the called: new habitual holiness
english: In the mercifully called, God dispels mental darkness, softens the hard heart, orders disordered appetites.
New holiness rises chiefly as an internal lasting habitual grace, not merely isolated good works.

title: Scripture: new creature, rebirth, Spirit renewal
english: Scripture: new creature, God's workmanship, born of God, seed remaining, raised from sin's death, renewed by the Spirit.
Change is moral—holy habits disposing to right, pious, just action—not a change of physical essence.

title: Partakers of divine nature; new man in true holiness
english: Believers are partakers of the divine nature; washed, sanctified, clothed with the new man in true justice and holiness.
This righteousness is real, not feigned—an image of divine holiness.

title: Renewed mind, new heart, flesh crucified
english: Scripture gives a renewed mind, light in the Lord, new heart and Spirit, flesh crucified with its lusts.
These pieces describe the Spirit-wrought holiness we affirm in the faithful.

title: Habitual and actual righteousness as good fruit
english: As a good tree bears good fruit, the renewed bear holy works also called righteousness.
Schools call the former habitual, the latter actual justice.

title: Believers called just and holy over against the wicked
english: Scripture often names believers just and holy over against the wicked.
Noah, Lot, Joseph of Arimathea are singled out as just.

title: Scripture names them just before God himself
english: Because Scripture is God's voice, those it names just from inherent righteousness are truly such before God, not only before men.
Luke 1:6: Zechariah and Elizabeth were just before God.

title: Spirit-wrought holiness is true and God-pleasing
english: Spirit-formed holiness is true sanctity of truth—not hypocrisy—and bears a likeness to divine justice.
Therefore it pleases God; Peter: in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is accepted.

title: God magnificently rewards this holiness
english: God richly rewards this holiness now and hereafter; piety has promise of this life and the next.
At the last judgment he will solemnly attest believers' righteousness and crown it with eternal life—the crown of righteousness.

title: True righteousness is infused, not humanly acquired
english: This God-pleasing justice differs from civil/human virtue gained by repeated acts.
It must be divinely infused; those who receive it are said to be vivified, regenerated, newly created.

title: God ordinarily prepares by preventing grace
english: Though none can reach or dispose himself to true holiness unaided, God ordinarily first prepares by preventing grace.
He excites inward acts and affections before creating that justice in the soul.

title: Preparatory acts: sense of sin, fear, faith, hope
english: Preparatory acts: sense and acknowledgment of sin, fear of judgment, purpose of better life, hatred of past sin, some hope and trust, love, above all efficacious faith.
Before sanctifying Spirit and habitual grace, one must believe, be stricken, and flee to mercy intending amendment.

title: Sanctifying Spirit promised only to believers and penitents
english: The sanctifying Spirit is promised only to believers and penitents—Jn 7; Acts 2:38.
One must hunger and thirst for righteousness before being filled—Matt 5:6.

title: Sanctification is free gift, not earned by prior acts
english: Prior acts do not merit or efficiently cause sanctification; it is God's free gift.
Rom 6:23ree gift of justifying/regenerating grace.

title: Regeneration not ex operibus per apostolic rule
english: Since regeneration is wholly of grace, it is not ex operibus by apostolic rule—Rom 11:6.
Grace and works as meritorious cause exclude each other.

title: Titus 3: salvation by mercy, not works of righteousness
english: The salvation we already share is chiefly freedom from sin's slavery and true holiness—yet Titus 3 denies it is from works of righteousness we did.
It is by mercy through washing of regeneration and Spirit renewal.

title: Eph 2: created in Christ for good works
english: Eph 2: made alive with Christ, saved by grace through faith, not of works; God's workmanship created for good works.
Grace both pardons and newly creates so we live justly afterward.

title: Inherent holiness never reaches the summit in this life
english: In this life inherent holiness never reaches the summit; it must always grow.
Paul near death had not attained; the Apocalypse still urges the just to be justified yet more.

title: Even the holy still stumble from weakness
english: Holiness is also spotted by many blemishes; the holy still fall from weakness.
Jas 3:2; 1 Jn 1:8; Eccl 7:20: no one on earth always does good without sinning.

title: Protestant imperfecta means incomplete in degree
english: When Protestants call inherent justice inchoate and imperfect, they mean it never reaches the highest degree on earth.
It must daily advance until consummated hereafter; the regenerate keep defects until death.

title: Incomplete in degree, complete in essential parts
english: Inchoate does not deny completeness of essence and integrating parts; imperfect does not mean lacking what belongs to true justice.
They distinguish perfection of degrees (denied here) from perfection of essential/integrating parts (affirmed).

title: Romans say perfect/absolute in essence, not degree
english: Roman doctors verbally reject inchoate/imperfect language, calling it perfect and absolute—yet when explained, they mean essence, not degree.
They admit remaining blemishes and need of mercy; absolute = truly such, not fictively.

title: Vasquez: perfect = nothing lacking to true justice
english: Vasquez: our justice is true and perfect because nothing needed for the ratio of justice is missing—not because it is at the highest degree.
He equates true with perfect as to essence, not degrees.

title: Bellarmine: infused virtues still need daily remission
english: Bellarmine: infused virtues are perfect in a way yet must daily be perfectedthey need daily remission of venials.
Habitual justice makes us just absolutely; actual justice is somehow imperfect by venial mixture.

title: Contarini: our inherent justice is inchoate and imperfect
english: Milder Romans (Contarini, Paris-approved) frankly call inherent justice inchoate and imperfect.
It cannot keep us from often offending.

title: No one stands the strict tribunal by inherent justice alone
english: Given imperfect inherent holiness and ongoing falls, no one can stand God's strict tribunal by his own justice and works alone.
Without indulgence, none would be cleared or judged worthy of eternal life.

title: Psalm, Job, and the Lord's Prayer prove the need of mercy
english: Ps 130:3; Job 9; Ps 143:2; and the daily Our Father prove all need mercy.
Even the holiest must pray forgive us our debts.

title: Rome too admits none can stand without divine pardon
english: Even strong assertors of inherent justice concede none can stand if God judges without mercy.
Gregory: all human justice is injustice under strict judgment; post-justification falls still need pardon.

title: Vasquez on Ps 142: even after justification, venials remain
english: Vasquez on Ps 142/143: the Psalmist rightly asks not to be judged without prior mercy.
Even after mortal-sin justification, uncleared venials would damn without mercy.

title: Contarini: lean on Christ's justice, not inherent grace
english: Contarini: when we think of judgment we must lean on Christ's donated justice as sure foundation—not on inherent holiness.
Inherent justice is inchoate and cannot keep us from continual sin.

title: Remission is free, not merited by inherent justice
english: Inherent holiness does not remove need of free pardon for sins before and after justification.
Remission is not merited by any justice or preparatory works in us.

title: Scripture: free forgiveness; Christ's passion the sole merit
english: Scripture: God freely forgives all offenses; we are saved/justified by grace, not works.
Christ's passion and obedience unto death is the sole merit moving God to pardon.

title: Trent: meritorious cause is Christ's passion alone
english: Romans agree first justification is free; Trent's sole meritorious cause is Christ's passion.
Nothing preceding justification—faith or works—merits the grace of justification.

title: Becanus and Bellarmine deny first justification from merits
english: Becanus: first justifying grace and remission are not from merits; dispositions do not merit them.
Bellarmine: we are not received for any merit in us or for inchoate newness as meritorious reconciliation.

title: Main dispute: are we formally justified by inherent justice?
english: Despite much agreement on nature of regenerate holiness, a heated question remains: are we formally justified before God by inherent justice?
Rome after Trent says yes; Protestants with great consent say no—minds must be stated clearly.

title: Protestants take justify forensically: absolve before God
english: Protestants take justify forensically: to be absolved and pronounced innocent before God under the law's strictnesstrictnesstrictness.
Denying justification by inherent justice means no one's own holiness clears him if God examines without mercy.

title: Yet they affirm true God-pleasing holiness in the regenerate
english: They do not deny true God-approved holiness in the regenerate—real before God, imaging divine virtues.
In the last evangelical judgment God will solemnly attest and reward it with eternal life.

title: Polish Confession: not justified forensically by inherent justice
english: Polish Confession: we deny being forensically justified by inherent justice so as to be cleared of death's guilt and declared heirs of life for it.
Broadly one may say infused virtues make us just/holy, yet that justice cannot stand the severe tribunal.

title: Davenant: inherent justice not formal cause of strict justification
english: Davenant allows calling inherent justice a formal cause in a loose sense, but not of justification that answers the Judge's strict exam.
Reformed sayings that none is just before God by inherent justice are comparative—not absolute denial of true holiness.

title: Rome takes justify morally as sanctify and cleanse
english: Rome takes justify morally as sanctify and cleanse from sin's filth.
Formal justification by inherent justice = Spirit-infused form naming and making them holy before God, lasting to final reward.

title: Rome denies standing the strict tribunal by inherent works
english: Rome does not claim inherent justice stands the severe tribunal without mercy.
Remission is free; some say faith/penance merit it de congruo—Stapleton and others refuse that phrase.

title: Verbal clash; substance often agrees on this head
english: On this question words clash, but the thing often agrees once ambiguous terms are removed.
Difficulty hangs on different uses of justificare.

title: Affined question: dispositions preparing for justification
english: Affined dispute: is the sinner prepared by certain works for justification? Rome yes, Protestants no—in words.
Rome means preventing grace excites prior acts of faith, hope, love, fear, sorrow, new-life purpose as conditions before habitual infusion.

title: Ames and thesis 16+: Reformed admit preparatory dispositions
english: This does not clash with Reformed teaching from thesis 16 onward.
Ames: in every convert after reason's use, some dispositions ordinarily precede, in varying amounts

title: Dordt British: external and internal preparatories
english: British at Dort: some external works ordinarily required before regeneration; also internal effects—knowledge of God's will, sense of sin, fear, hope of pardon.
As natural generation has prior dispositions, so spiritual birth follows many antecedent grace-acts.

title: Caveat: not by free will or meritorious works
english: Reformed carefully deny that natural free will can prepare for grace, or that any works—even grace-aided—merit remission or the Spirit.
That is what they fight when opposing Roman preparation-talk.

title: Dispositions allowed if not efficient or meritorious causes
english: Otherwise they gladly allow many prerequisites before forensic justification/remission, call them dispositions if not efficient or meritorious causes.
Sense, acknowledgment, detestation of sin, fear, desire and hope of grace, some love—Acts 3:19.

title: Paraeus, Ames, British: prior conditions, not causing causes
english: Paraeus: dispositions may precede justification; justification is not acquired by them as causes.
Ames and the British: prior conditions under the Word, not sudden enthusiasm—Acts 2:37.

title: Davenant: concurrent conditions, not meritorious causes
english: Davenant: some good works are necessary as accompanying or preliminary conditions, not as efficient or meritorious causescausescauses.
Mercy does not justify logs or stubborn mules but contrite followers of Word and Spirit—like a patient cooperating yet healed by the physician's remedy (Christ's blood).

title: Protestants deny only free-will or meritorious dispositions
english: Protestants do not simply deny all preparatory dispositions before justification in either school's sense.
They deny only dispositions ascribed to free will's powers or counted as efficient/meritorious causes.

title: Most Romans deny natural or congruous merit of first grace
english: Most Roman doctors deny such meritorious natural dispositions—Trent: nothing preceding merits justification grace; dispositions are from preventing grace.
Stapleton: not from our powers; not even de congruo; pure moral works do not prepare for Christian justice.

title: On dispositions: real agreement; only a logomachy remains
english: Since Protestants allow moral conditions/dispositions before justification, and Rome does not make them efficient/meritorious causes—the one point Protestants solely reject—no real controversy remains, only a logomachy.

title: Fallen man freed only by free divine pardon
english: Once guilty of eternal death, man cannot escape sin’s due penalty or gain eternal life except by God’s free pardon and acceptance.

title: God is merciful yet also just
english: God’s nature is merciful toward the wretched, yet also just.
Mercy urges pardon; justice forbids leaving sin unpunished.

title: Pardon requires satisfaction somehow taken
english: Divine wisdom will not pardon without justice satisfied and a fitting penalty somehow exacted.

title: Sinner cannot be both remitted and condignly punished
english: The same sinner cannot both receive remission and undergo sin’s full condign penalty.
Eternal death’s desert bars simultaneous salvation and exacted punishment in him alone.

title: A surety must bear the owed penalty
english: Mercy and justice both require a surety onto whom men’s due penalty is transferred.

title: Surety must be man, yet without our guilt
english: The surety must be human—punishment in the nature that sinned—yet not himself under our common guilt.

title: Mere man cannot bear infinite curse-weight
english: A bare man would sink under the divine curse and cannot equal the race’s desert.
The Surety must be both God and man.

title: God sent the eternal Son as Mediator-surety
english: God sent his eternal Son—true God and true man—as Mediator and surety.
He exhausts our due penalties, turns wrath, and satisfies divine justice for us.

title: Incarnate Son obedient unto the cross
english: At the prophesied time the Son took servant form, sinless human weakness, and holy life.
Willingly he obeyed unto cursed, shameful cross-death in our name.

title: Isaiah 53 foretold the Messiah’s passion for us
english: Isaiah 53, speaking future as past, depicts the Messiah bearing our griefs and iniquity.
Wounded for our transgressions; by his bruise we are healed; soul poured out for many.

title: Peter and Paul: just for unjust; made a curse
english: Peter: Christ suffered, the just for the unjust, bearing our sins on the tree.
Paul: made a curse for us—cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.

title: Christ’s death as sacrifice and redemption-price
english: Scripture casts Christ’s death as expiating sacrifice and redeeming price.
He gave himself as ransom; we are bought with his precious blood, not gold.

title: Satisfaction by a surety is imputed to the debtor
english: Deny imputation only if you deny Christ’s death satisfied for our sins.
A surety’s accepted payment is imputed to the debtor in whose name it was made.

title: Imputed obedience alone absolves and adopts
english: Christ’s donated, imputed obedience is the sole righteousness that absolves and adopts.
By it we escape due perdition and become heirs of eternal life.

title: Inherent holiness given with remission, not its meritorious cause
english: God never absolves without also clothing in true habitual holiness growing toward future perfection.
That inherent righteousness is not the meritorious cause of remission or adoption—both are free gifts for Christ’s sake.

title: Living faith and repentance required, yet not meritorious
english: God requires living faith and serious repentance before imputing Christ’s merit.
Those acts are prerequisite conditions, not meritorious causes—grace remains wholly free for Christ’s sake.

title: Scripture: justified freely by Christ’s blood
english: Scripture repeatedly: saved and justified freely by Christ’s blood, not by works.
Rom 3, Eph 2, Tit 3: grace, redemption, propitiation, heirs by mercy.

title: Redeemed from curse; made God’s righteousness in him
english: Christ became a curse; God made him sin that we become God’s righteousness in him.
He is our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption; one obedience constitutes many just.

title: What Reformed mean by imputed Christ’s righteousness
english: Reformed “imputed righteousness” means Christ’s cross-obedience given as truly ours—the sole ground of absolution and adoption.
No inherent works can stand law’s rigor; conscience flees only to Christ’s merit.

title: Faith, repentance, and renovating grace not denied
english: Imputation does not cancel required living faith and sincere repentance.
Christ also merited renovating grace; inherent holiness, though imperfect, is accepted and promised glory.

title: Polish deputies at Thorn: justify and sanctify together
english: Thorn Polish declaration: for Christ’s alone-imputed merit God absolves and adopts.
At once by poured-out charity he renews and sanctifies unto new obedience.

title: Calumny rejected: inherent justice not denied
english: False charge: Reformed deny all inherent justice and teach bare external imputation.
We impute only to living faith with Spirit-wrought renovation; imperfect inherent justice cannot absolve at the judgment seat.

title: Called just from inherent form; justified by imputed
english: Scripture’s “just/holy” names ordinarily from inherent renewed holiness as a formal designationnn.
Yet they are justified and constituted just through Christ’s imputed obedience.

title: Davenant: just from inherent; justified from imputed
english: Davenant: “just” from inherent inchoate form; “justified” from Christ’s perfect imputed righteousness.
All justified receive infused habitual justice by which God also calls them just.

title: Rome distorts Reformed denial of inherent formal justification
english: Rome hears “justified by imputed, not inherent” and charges denial of all inward holiness.
Calumny: believers stay impure within; imputation only covers, never removes, sin.

title: Becanus’s five-point caricature of Calvinists
english: Becanus’s Calvinist cartoon: sins covered not removed; no infused justice; man stays impious within.
All works mortal sins under a cover; justification = concealment only.

title: Reformed confess inherent justice and a secondary formal sense
english: Rome fights a monster we do not teach: we confess Spirit-cleansing and infused inherent justice.
Besides forensic absolution we allow with Davenant/Poles a secondary formal justification by inherent virtue.

title: Why inherent justice cannot justify at the severe bar
english: Denial of inherent formal justification means: none stand law’s rigor without mercy.
Freedom and adoption are owed solely to Christ’s communicated passion-merit, not our works’ dignity.

title: Genuine Reformed imputation doctrine Rome dare not openly deny
english: Plain Reformed imputation is so clear that Rome dare not openly deny it when simply stated.

title: Stapleton and Vasquez: none stand without mercy
english: No Roman doctor dares claim inherent justice stands God’s severe bar without mercy.
Stapleton and Vasquez: say with the Psalmist—enter not into judgment; venials still need mercy.

title: Trent: remission and adoption free; no preceding works merit
english: Rome too: all need free remission and adoption; Trent Sess. 6.8—nothing preceding merits justifying grace.
Justification includes remission plus sanctifying renovation; benefits are gratis.

title: Trent’s meritorious cause is Christ’s passion—same as our imputation
english: Trent: meritorious cause is Christ’s cross-passion communicated—else none is just.
That is what Reformed mean by imputing Christ’s righteousness: free remission and adoption by his alone-communicated merit.

title: Bellarmine allows imputation in a sound sense—ours
english: Rome concedes a sound sense of imputing Christ’s righteousness—as becoming ours.
Bellarmine: if heretics mean donated merits we may offer the Father, the opinion is right.

title: Bellarmine: Christ our righteousness by donated satisfaction
english: Bellarmine: Christ is our righteousness because his satisfaction is donated as ours in justifying us.
Inherent justice is an effect of that satisfaction; imputation language is fine if inherent justice is not denied.

title: Vasquez: Trent’s communicantur equals imputantur
english: Vasquez: Trent’s “communicated” passion-merits = “imputed.”
As meritorious cause, imputation means the application and communicationnicationnication of Christ’s merits.

title: Our imputation means satisfaction’s effect—not denial of inherent justice
english: Imputation language means: donated satisfaction is ours; remission is its alone effect—not inherent justice’s merit.
We still confess real though imperfect inherent holiness; Rome’s attack is undeserved.

title: Whether glory is due inherent justice: deferred; promise by fittingness
english: Whether glory is strictly due inherent justice is deferred to merits; works per se are owed nothing.
God promised the crown and will keep it by fitting goodness and promise-faithfulness—as saner Rome grants.

title: Scripture clearly teaches sin is taken away in the justified
english: Among Christians it is settled that God takes away sin in those he receives into grace.
Scripture teaches this so plainly that no one who respects its authority can doubt it.

title: Scripture: God removes, transfers, deletes, casts sins into the sea
english: Scripture often says God takes away, transfers, deletes, even casts the faithful's sins into the sea (Exodus 34; Micah 7).
Micah's sea-image alludes to Egypt drowned in the Red Sea.

title: Isaiah and David: God blots out iniquities; Acts calls to repentance
english: Isaiah 43-44: God blots out iniquities and will not remember sins.
David (Psalm 51) and Peter (Acts 3) seek and invite that blotting-out.

title: Christ the Lamb takes away the world's sins
english: John the Baptist calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sins (John 1).
1 John and Hebrews teach he appeared and was offered once to abolish many's sins.

title: Sin's two aspects: foulness and obligation to penalty
english: Sin has two sides: moral foulness that stains and God-hates, and obligation to the law's due penalty.

title: Christ's grace frees from due penalty; cross bears curse (Isa 53)
english: Christ's grace frees serious seekers from sin's due eternal-death obligation.
As our surety he bore cross-penalties—the just for the unjust—and redeemed from the law's curse (Isaiah 53:5-6).

title: Remission is not bare penalty-relaxation while we stay unrenewed
english: Cross-remission is not a prince's bare stay of punishment while the sinner stays inwardly unchanged.

title: God frees from penalty only while correcting foulness by the Spirit
english: God never frees from penalty without also correcting sin's foulness by repentance and the Spirit.
Christ suffered both to spare due punishment and to make the impious just and holy.

title: Paul and Peter: Christ gave himself to rescue and make us live to him
english: Christ gave himself to rescue us from this evil age and make the living live for him (Galatians 1; 2 Corinthians 5).
Peter and Titus tie his bearing of sins to dead-to-sin, sober, pious, just life.

title: Scripture paints sin as defiling filth from the heart (Mark 7; Rev 22)
english: Grace's efficacy is imaged against sin's filth: what comes from the heart defiles (Mark 7).
Revelation 22 warns the filthy to stay filthy—sin as abominable uncleanness before God.

title: God washes and cleanses: Ezekiel, Titus, Ephesians, 1 Cor, Psalm 51
english: Taking away sin's malice means washing and cleansing (Ezekiel 36; Titus 2; Ephesians 5).
Corinthians were washed, sanctified, justified (1 Corinthians 6); David begged hyssop-washing (Psalm 51).

title: Sin as slavery; Christ redeems into liberty and service of righteousness
english: Scripture casts indulged sin as hard slavery (John 8; 2 Peter).
Christ redeems captives into liberty; under grace sin no longer masters—old man crucified, servants of righteousness (Romans 6).

title: Sin as disease; healed by grace and Christ's bruise (Ps 103; Mal 4)
english: Sin is also disease and wound; God heals infirmities (Psalm 103).
By Christ's bruise we are healed; Malachi's sun of righteousness brings healing in his wings (Malachi 4).

title: Sin as death; grace vivifies with Christ (Eph 2; Col 2)
english: Sin is also death; grace raises us into new life with Christ (Ephesians 2; Colossians 2).
Baptismal burial with Christ means rising with him.

title: Grace removes both reatus and macula—else washing language fails
english: Grace removes sin both as reatus (penalty-obligation) and as macula (soul-infecting foulness).
Mere penalty-relaxation without cleansing would leave us still enslaved, sick, and dead—unable to be called washed or Spirit-walkers.

title: Cleansing is gradual; perfect holiness grows (2 Cor 7; Rev 22)
english: Cleansing is not once-for-all total; it advances by degrees.
Paul urges sharers of grace to perfect sanctification (2 Corinthians 7); Revelation 22: the righteous and holy still grow.

title: Washed disciples still need foot-washing; sanctify them in truth
english: Even the blood-washed still gather foot-dust and need ongoing cleansing (John 13).
Christ prays the Father to sanctify already-clean disciples in the truth of the word (John 17).

title: Native corruption remains fractured but not eradicated in this life
english: Native corruption's remains stay in mortal life: fractured so they no longer reign or damn the grafted-in, yet not eradicated.
Believers feel strong evil-tilt and flesh-Spirit war until death.

title: Vicious habits from past sins still incline the pious
english: Remitted past sins still leave vicious habits that boost inborn corruption and push even the pious toward fresh sins.
Grace slowly deletes those habits but does not yet fully uproot them.

title: Justified still stumble daily (James, Eccl, Prov, 1 John)
english: Even the justified stumble daily from weakness (James 3; Ecclesiastes 7; Proverbs 20).
1 John 1: claiming sinlessness is self-deceit.

title: Purged yet residual weakness; sin no longer reigns but leftovers remain
english: Grace purges stain and breaks disease-force—out of death's danger—yet residual languor remains.
Sin no longer reigns; its strength wears down daily, but leftovers demand continual fight.

title: Reformed mean: sin remains (not imputed) yet true cleansing and inherent justice
english: When Reformed say sin remains (unimputed, covered), they do not mean the justified stay unrenewed wallowers.
God truly cleanses and gifts inherent justice; yet daily debts and innate concupiscence remain to fight.

title: Concupiscence is sin broadly (ψεικτόν); strict forensic sense distinguished (Davenant/Augustine)
english: Reformed call remaining concupiscence sin in the broad moral sense—blameworthy ψεκτόν against creation's order.
Strictly (Augustine/Davenant) it is not always forensic guilt-obliging sin; the broad/strict distinction reconciles Augustine.

title: Roman calumny: Reformed allegedly teach only covering, not real removal
english: Rome (Becanus, Vasquez) charges that Reformed leave the justified inwardly unclean with only alien cover, even mortal works hidden.
Hold the orthodox explanation against that calumny.

title: We confess real purification into piety, justice, and holy works
english: We freely confess God truly purges the justified from sin into piety, justice, and holiness.
The Spirit makes them deny ungodliness and bear repentance-worthy works.

title: Yet something of sin remains; even Rome must grant this
english: We still hold that in this life some sin remains in the justified, who always need mercy.
Even Roman doctors are forced to grant that explored truth.

title: Rome grants daily venials coexist with justifying grace (Bellarmine)
english: Rome admits no one ordinarily lives sinless; daily lighter sins coexist with justifying grace.
Bellarmine vs Pelagians: grace is cast off by graver flesh-works, not by those venials.

title: Rome: remitted sins' stain wiped, yet vicious habits remain to be deleted
english: Rome says remission wipes the whole leftover stain, yet admits vicious habits remain after remitted acts.
Those habits are slowly deleted by grace—and that is part of sanctification progress (Bellarmine).

title: After original sin remitted, material fomes/concupiscence remains
english: Even after original sin's remission, Rome keeps the 'material'—proneness to evil, difficulty in good, nature's disorder.
That is scholastic concupiscence or fomes: the lower powers rebelebelebel; the whole man tilts to evil.

title: Remaining concupiscence is morally blameworthy and to be crucified
english: Rome grants remaining concupiscence opposes the law and is moral vice to bridle, destroy, and crucify.
Progress in that fight marks greater perfection and sanctity.

title: God hates concupiscence without hating the regenerate person (Bellarmine duplex odium)
english: Rome: God hates remaining concupiscence as a displeasing thing, yet not with hatred that damns the person (Trent 'hates nothing in the regenerate')erate')erate').
Bellarmine: God consumes it gradually so the regenerate are healed—not damned for it.

title: Rome allows improper 'sin' for concupiscence; little distance from Protestants
english: Rome denies proper 'sin' for regenerate concupiscence yet allows broader/improper sin-language (from sin, to sin, disordered lower powers).
That reading covers Paul's Romans usage (Bellarmine)—so Rome stands little off from Protestants while still railing bitterly.

title: Roman calumny: Protestants make absolute certainty of pardon the essence of justifying faith
english: Romans often charge that Protestants make a firm persuasion of personal pardon the essence of saving faith.
They claim this certainty must match assent to Christ’s deity, that without it no one is truly faithful, and that it alone justifies even those who are wickedre wicked.

title: Bellarmine and Becanus especially fasten these charges; this disputation answers by Reformed sense
english: Bellarmine and Becanus especially pin these charges on the Reformed.
This disputation answers them by the same clear exposition already used on justification.

title: No one may rightly claim justification without heartfelt renunciation of worldly vices
english: Reformed doctrine first denies lawful assurance to anyone still clinging to unrepented vice.
Claims of pardon without serious repentance are Satanic security, not gospel mercy.

title: Those who repent and obey in true faith may be secure of God’s mercy and of remitted sins
english: Serious penitents who trust Christ and obey him may be secure of mercy and remitted sins.
The holiness they pursue is accepted by God unto eternal life.

title: David’s Psalms show saintly confidence of righteousness and eternal life before God
english: David’s Psalms display confident assurance of righteousness and eternal life before God.
Psalm 17 and 103 especially voice forgiveness, healing, and redemption as present mercies.

title: Hezekiah near death dares to plead his piety and integrity before God
english: Hezekiah, near death, still confides in grace and dares to recall his sincere walk before God.

title: Paul often speaks as wholly secure of God’s kindness and of Christ living in him
english: Paul often speaks as secure of God’s mercy and of Christ living in him.
Galatians 2 and the Pastorals voice obtained mercy and a laid-up crown of righteousness.

title: Scripture shows ordinary believers, not only especial saints, may be certain they are in grace
english: Assurance is not a rare privilege of a few saints; Scripture gives it to all living believers.
Romans 8’s witness of the Spirit, self-examination in 2 Corinthians 13, and 1 John 5’s knowing eternal life show ordinary certainty is possible.

title: The Spirit’s peace and joy in believers imply persuasion of divine favor
english: Spirit-wrought peace and joy cannot sit with doubt that one is accepted by God.
Believers who taste that joy may rightly conclude they stand in grace.

title: Certainty of the indwelling Spirit entails certainty of justification
english: If one knows the Spirit dwells within, one cannot doubt true justifying faith.
Paul and John treat the gift of the Spirit as a known mark of abiding in Christ.

title: Paul’s command to prove whether Christ is in us implies discernible marks of living faith
english: Self-examination would be pointless if living faith had no certain marks.
Christ’s indwelling yields a sense of himself clear enough for believers to read.

title: Constant thanksgiving for remitted sins is absurd without certainty of the gift
english: Believers must thank God for remission and rescue in Christ.
Thanksgiving without certainty of the gift is mockery, not gratitude.

title: Those in grace not only may but ought to be certain; doubt marks weak faith
english: Those in grace ought to be certain of it, not merely able to be.
Wavering about grace signals weak faith, a fault to be amended.

title: Spiritual joy in Christ is both Spirit’s fruit and believers’ commanded duty
english: Joy in Christ requires certainty of grace and is both Spirit-fruit and commanded duty.
Philippians 4 and Romans 12 make rejoicing a standing office of the faithful.

title: Perfect love casts out fear; doubt of justification cannot coexist with perfect charity
english: Perfect love drives out punitive fear; lingering doubt of grace cannot coexist with it.
John’s teaching makes uncertainty about one’s justification a defect charity excludes.

title: Bold access to the throne of grace is incompatible with uncertainty whether God is appeased
english: Scripture bids bold access to grace’s throne.
Uncertainty whether God is for or against us yields only anxious fear, not confidence.

title: Doubt of grace marks weak faith, yet does not cast one out of the number of true believers
english: Some doubt of one’s grace is a fault of weak faith, not proof of unbelief.
Certainty scales with the strength of faith.

title: Many true believers lack full certainty before death because they look too much at their unworthiness
english: Sincere believers may lack full certainty even until death.
The cause is fixation on personal unworthiness, not distrust of God’s promises.

title: Prophets themselves were tossed with doubts about God’s favor, as the Psalms show
english: The Psalms record prophets tossed by doubts about God’s abiding mercy.
Psalms 77 and 88 voice fear that God has cast off and shut up his compassions.

title: Such prophetic doubt is infirmity to fight, not virtue to imitate; make calling sure by good works
english: Prophetic doubt is weakness to resist, not humility to cultivate.
Fight it by Word, prayer, and holiness, making calling sure by good works.

title: Absolute trust that pardon is already obtained is not the essential formal act of justifying faith
english: Weak true faith can temporarily lack absolute assurance of already-obtained pardon.
Therefore that assurance is not faith’s essential formal act.

title: Assurance of already-received pardon presupposes prior faith and arises from sensing that faith
english: Assurance that pardon is already mine reasons from sensed living faith; it follows faith.
Faith’s formal act constitutes faith; it does not arise from reflecting on faith already there.

title: Assurance of already being justified is posterior to justification; justifying faith’s act is prior
english: Persuasion that one is already justified comes after justification itself.
The act of justifying faith comes naturally first, since faith is the means of justification.

title: Two fiduciae: refuge-adherence (essence of living faith) versus sense-assurance (fruit, not always felt)
english: Learned Reformed distinguish refuge-trust (faith’s essence and instrument) from sense-assurance (a fruit not always felt).
Salvation does not necessarily hang on the felt persuasion of already-obtained pardon.

title: Two doubts answer the two trusts: deadly doubt of the promise versus non-mortal doubt of one’s own faith
english: Doubt of the promise’s truth kills faith; doubt of one’s own interest, born of sensed weakness, can coexist with true though languid faith.
James 1’s warning targets the first doubt, not the second.

title: Certainty of one’s justification is not the same kind as certainty of revealed articles of faith
english: Dogmatic certainty about revealed articles is necessary to remaining a believer.
Personal certainty that I am justified is not of the same kind and is not itself a dogma of faith.

title: Why Reformed call assurance ‘certainty of faith’: it rests partly on a revealed premise, partly on experience
english: Reformed call assurance ‘certainty of faith’ because one premise is revealed and the other is experiential self-knowledge of living faith.
Not everything referred to faith’s assent shares the same necessity as truths resting wholly on divine testimony.

title: In saving faith distinguish the direct act (embracing Christ) from the reflex act (recognizing one’s faith)
english: Assurance is not justifying faith’s formal act, yet may be called a reflex secondary act of that faith.
The direct act embraces Christ; the reflex act reads one’s own faith and its fruits.

title: The persuasion treated here is reflex, secondary, for faith’s perfection—not justification’s instrument
english: Assurance is a reflex secondary act for faith’s perfection, not its essence.
It follows justification already made and cannot be justification’s instrumental condition.

title: As faith grows or weakens, so the sense of God’s favor and our standing in grace strengthens or fades
english: Assurance tracks faith’s vigor: as faith grows, confidence of divine favor strengthens; as faith flags, assurance softens.

title: Roman doctors preface object- vs subject-certainty; the question concerns the latter
english: Roman doctors begin with Bellarmine’s distinction between certainty of the object and of the believing subject.
Object-certainty is the thing’s immutability; subject-certainty is firm assent without doubt—and that latter sense is the one at issue here.

title: Assent may be firm yet groundless; true certainty needs a legitimate foundation in the thing
english: Firm assent without a real foundation is persuasion, not true certainty.
This controversy concerns only certainty that is both firm and legitimately grounded in the thing.

title: Evident certainty: first principles, scientific conclusions, and sense experience
english: Schools divide true certainty into evident and obscure, each with three grades.
Evident certainty runs from self-evident principles through scientific conclusions to sense experience.

title: Obscure certainty: divine faith, then moral human faith that excludes rash doubt
english: Obscure certainty begins with divine faith, to which no falsehood can attach.
Next is moral or human-faith certainty—like believing famous cities exist—strong enough that contrary doubt is rash, though not absolutely infallible.

title: Conjectural certainty: signs that secure the mind without banishing all fear
english: Lowest obscure certainty is conjectural: many signs quiet anxiety without removing every fear.
Handwriting recognition and medical diagnosis illustrate this opinion-level certainty.

title: Catholic vs private faith-certainty: public revelation versus private disclosure
english: Romans split faith-certainty into Catholic (public Church revelation) and private (personal revelation).
Only the former binds all as the common object of faith.

title: Even conjectural certainty excludes doubt proper, which suspends judgment
english: For Romans even the lowest certainty still excludes doubt proper.
Doubt suspends assent; certainty, even conjectural, determinately takes one side.

title: Doubt vs fear: determinate assent may remain with fear that things could be otherwise
english: Romans separate doubt (suspended judgment) from fear (firm assent that still allows the opposite).
Recognizing a familiar signature can be certain yet still admit fear of clever forgery.

title: Vasquez: fear can accompany determinate opinion; doubt is hesitation between both sides
english: Vasquez defines doubt as intellective hesitation between contradictories.
Fear is a reflex judgment that principles might fail—compatible with firm opinionated assent.

title: Doubt taken strictly vs broadly: Romans sometimes call fear itself ‘doubt’
english: Proper doubt is more than fear, yet Romans often stretch ‘doubt’ to cover fear.
Strict doubt freezes assent; broad doubt can coexist with choosing one side.

title: Faith-certainty vs hope/trust-certainty: promise alone versus promise plus disposition
english: Faith-certainty hangs on God’s promise alone and excludes even fear.
Hope-certainty also weighs one’s own disposition, so it is only moral or conjectural and may retain some fear while still banishing fluctuating doubt.

title: Bellarmine: adversaries confuse faith-certainty with trust-certainty
english: Bellarmine charges Protestants with confusing faith-certainty and trust-certainty.
Trust is absolute on the promise side but only conjectural about one’s disposition, yet still enough for security; faith’s certainty touches intellect alone.

title: Stapleton: heretics’ faith-certainty vs Catholics’ hope-certainty; moral certainty suffices for peace
english: Stapleton distinguishes Protestant ‘faith-certainty’ of pardon from Catholic hope-certainty.
Hope is infallible on God’s promise, weaker about one’s disposition, yet still a firm moral certainty—not endless anxious fluctuation.

title: Romans agree the just can have some certainty without special revelation; they differ on its kind
english: All Roman doctors grant the truly just some real certainty of grace without special revelation.
They disagree on its grade; Bellarmine counts three Catholic opinions.

title: First opinion (Catharinus): private divine-faith certainty of one’s justification without special revelation
english: Catharinus allows private divine-faith certainty of being in grace without special revelation.
He argues that revealed sacramental principles plus evident experience of proper dispositionionion yield a divine-faith conclusion about one’s justification.

title: Catharinus hard to square with Trent sess. 6 cap. 9; commonly rejected after the Council
english: Trent session 6 chapter 9 denies faith-certainty that one has obtained grace.
After Trent Catharinus’s view is commonly rejected, though he still claimed the Council did not condemn him.

title: Second opinion: perfect just may reach moral certainty excluding fear, like historical human faith
english: The second Roman view denies divine-faith certainty of grace but allows moral certainty without fear.
It likens that security to our firm historical belief about Caesar, Virgil, or distant cities never seen.

title: Vasquez assigns the moral-certainty view to Soto, Vega, and Tapper
english: Vasquez ties the moral-certainty line to Soto, Vega, and Tapper.
Tapper allows that clear spiritual signs can yield fearless though not infallible certainty of present grace.

title: Vega’s signs: deathbed desire for Christ, martyrs’ joy, Bernard on sudden conversion
english: Vega points to peaceful deaths, longing to be with Christ, and martyrs’ joy as signs of moral certainty of grace.
Bernard’s sudden conversion under heavenly light likewise yields fearless assurance short of strict faith-certainty.

title: Moral certainty excluding fear rejected by most Romans as clashing with Trent’s ‘may fear’
english: Most Roman theologians now reject fear-excluding moral certainty of grace.
Trent’s ‘anyone may fear regarding his grace’ is taken to bar certainty that banishes all fear.

title: Third and commonest opinion: only conjectural hope-certainty joined with some fear
english: The common Roman third view allows only conjectural hope-certainty of one’s justification.
Some fear remains, yet fluctuating doubt is expelled enough for peace of conscience—absent special revelation.

title: Bellarmine prefers the middle way: no perpetual doubt, yet not faith-certainty of pardon
english: Bellarmine rejects both Catharinus’s faith-certainty and fearless moral security.
His middle way clears anxious doubt while still denying divine-faith certainty; penitential signs yield persuasion, not Catholic faith-certainty.

title: Stapleton’s analogies: moral/hope certainty of pardon without faith-certainty or endless fluctuation
english: Stapleton compares assurance of pardon to certainty of crowning, inheritance, safe travel, or one’s baptism—moral/hope certainty, not faith-certainty.
Catholics claim a middle path: firm hope on the promises plus dispositional signs, without Protestant absolute security or endless fluctuation.

title: Vasquez’s close: determinate true assent yes; fearless or infallible faith-certainty no
english: Vasquez sums up: the just may have determinate true assent about grace.
He denies both fearless assent and infallible faith-certainty in this debate’s sense of ‘certainty.’

title: How Roman doctors seem to contradict themselves: divine-faith doubt vs conjectural certainty
english: Roman polemic sounds self-contradictory: sometimes allowing certainty, sometimes calling the faithful doubtful.
The key is equivocation—denying divine-faith certainty while granting conjectural certainty, and calling residual fear ‘doubt’ in a broad sense.

title: Romans teach the just not only may but ought to be firmly persuaded of remission
english: Roman doctors say the justified ought to be firmly persuaded of pardon, not left in double-mindedness.
Assurance should grow with holiness; inability to trust adoption marks infirmity, not the perfect’s norm.

title: Vasquez: Trent allows fearing, not doubting; the just must absolutely believe they are in grace for the sacraments
english: Roman authorities insist the prudent just must not live in suspended doubt about grace.
Vasquez reads Trent as allowing fear, not doubt, and requires absolute belief one is in grace to use the sacraments.

title: Stapleton denies the calumny: penitents should by certain trust, not by infallible faith, judge sins remitted
english: Stapleton rejects the charge that Catholics strand penitents in endless doubt.
Penitents should judge sins remitted by certain trust of hope, not by infallible faith-certainty.

title: Roman ‘doubt’ targets application and disposition, not God’s promised benevolence in general
english: Romans do not distrust God’s general promised mercy; their caution concerns personal disposition and application.
They want firm assent from examined signs of faith and repentance, admitting residual fear—much as many Protestants distinguish direct and reflex certainty.

title: Shared ground: Roman and Protestant doctors agree the living faithful can and ought to trust their reconciliation
english: On Le Blanc’s reading the live dispute is not whether justified believers may firmly trust their reconciliation.
Roman doctors openly teach that living faith both can and ought to yield certain persuasion of pardon—common ground with Protestants.

title: Doubt whether one is in grace is a defect to fight, not a virtue to foster
english: Roman doctors do not praise lingering doubt about one’s gracious standing.
With Stapleton they treat such hesitation as a defect and temptation to be fought—especially when no unrepented grave sin accuses the conscience.

title: No dispute that certainty of justification suffices for peace and thanksgiving
english: Both sides grant that justified believers’ certainty can quiet anxiety and underwrite thanksgiving.
Roman doctors do not deny that such trust belongs to peace of conscience.

title: Full persuasion of pardon is not so necessary that the weak of faith are cut off
english: Protestants do not make absolute assurance of pardon the gate of true faith.
Weak believers who still fear may remain truly faithful and reconciled in Christ.

title: No warrant to claim justification while persisting in unrepented sin
english: Neither school licenses presuming justification while clinging to unrepented sin.
Protestants tie true assurance to a good conscience and love’s fruits, not carnal security.

title: Certainty arises from promise plus inward sense of living faith and repentance
english: Assurance is not bare assent to general gospel promises.
It requires the reflective subsumption: I myself have the living, loving faith God requires.

title: Even strong certainty keeps company with pious solicitude, not carnal security
english: Mature assurance still keeps a godly fear of solicitude.
Protestants cast out distrustful fear, not the watchful fear that wars against carnal security.

title: Assurance of one’s justification is not the same necessity as assent to articles of faith
english: Doubting a gospel article unbelief; doubting one’s own sincerity need not.
Protestants refuse to equate assurance of status with assent to the creed.

title: Trust in pardon already obtained is not the formal act of justifying faith; hope of mercy is required
english: Justifying faith’s prior act is refuge-trust toward mercy, not assurance of pardon already sealed.
Trent itself requires hope of pardon in the disposing sinner—common ground Le Blanc presses.

title: Vasquez: private faith of the promise, with hope of pardon, is needed for justification
english: Vasquez requires more than catholic assent to general promises.
A private faith that God will not fail me—and hope of pardon—belongs to the disposition for justification.

title: Cologne Catholics once spoke like some Protestants about certain belief of personal pardon
english: Even sixteenth-century Cologne Catholics once urged certain personal belief of pardon.
Le Blanc notes both Rome and many Reformed now refuse to make already-granted reconciliation the prior act of justifying faith.

title: The live dispute: is assurance certainty of divine faith, or only of hope/conjecture?
english: The real clash is nomenclature and grade: divine-faith certainty versus hope’s moral or conjectural certainty.
Rome (almost unanimously) ranks status-assurance below article-faith; Protestants commonly call it faith’s certainty.

title: Roman denial of divine-faith certainty often means unequal firmness/necessity, not total absence
english: Rome’s denial often means: status-assurance lacks the firmness and necessity of creed-articles.
Both sides still allow a syllogism from gospel promise plus sincere inward faith-signs.

title: Much of the fight is logomachy over calling assurance divine-faith certainty
english: Shared foundations, quarreling labels: Protestants still say ‘divine faith’; Rome refuses because of the weaker experiential premise.
Le Blanc flags a classic verbal dispute under the syllogism’s weaker-part rule.

title: Vega allows calling it faith’s certainty if not equated with catholic dogmatic certainty
english: Vega softens the label: call it faith’s certainty if you refuse equality with catholic dogma.
Trent (on his reading) blocks ‘certainty of faith,’ not every knowing ‘through faith.’

title: Vasquez elsewhere ranks believing oneself justified as a species of private faith
english: Vasquez’s anti-Catharinus zeal sits oddly beside his own ‘private faith’ taxonomy.
He lists believing oneself justified among non-catholic faith-species tied to God’s gift.

title: Even amid equivocation, a real split remains vs. those who allow only conjectural certainty
english: Word-fights with moral-certainty Romanists can be largely verbal.
The hard disagreement is with conjectural-only doctors who never shut out fear of deception.

title: Roman doctors still admit true fixed assent that yields peace—and redefine leftover fear
english: Rome grants fixed, peace-giving assent that one is in grace.
Their leftover ‘fear’ is about knowledge itself: I am not deceived—yet I do not believe deception is impossible.

title: Reformed also refuse creed-grade certainty and keep Calvin’s struggle with unbelief
english: Reformed refuse to equate status-assurance with creed-assent and keep watchful fear.
Calvin’s Antidote—faith fights unbelief—lets Le Blanc draw the parties near.

title: Stapleton-style residual fallibility does not make every non-faith assent fearful
english: Grant Stapleton’s fallibility note about self-judgment—deny that it makes ordinary certainties ‘fearful.’
Only God’s speech yields impossibility-of-falsehood; that bar would absurdly frighten snow-white and geometry.

title: Vasquez’s standing ‘perhaps otherwise’ judgment cancels even conjectural certainty
english: A live ‘perhaps I’m wrong’ veto is incompatible even with conjectural certainty.
Ordinary moral certainty says ‘doubtless thus,’ while still admitting absolute possibility otherwise.

title: Complaint: Roman doctors are not consistent when answering Protestant charges
english: Under Protestant fire Rome grants peace-giving moral or conjectural certainty and a duty to pursue it.
Le Blanc’s complaint is inconsistency with how they speak when on the attack.

title: Yet against Protestants they argue believers cannot safely judge their faith sincere
english: In polemic they stress radical uncertainty about one’s own sincerity.
Self-examination, they say, yields many grounds for doubt—and rashness if one settles the question.

title: They reconcile by narrowing ‘uncertain’ to lack of divine-faith certainty, and ‘doubt’ to fear
english: Their harmonizing move: ‘ignorant’ means lacking divine-faith certainty; ‘doubt’ means fear.
Le Blanc calls that either contradiction or verbal abuse.

title: Absurd to call someone ignorant of what he knows by sense, proof, or common fame
english: Lack of divine-faith certainty does not license the word ‘ignorance.’
Demonstration, sense, and common fame still yield knowledge in ordinary speech.

title: Nor may we say a physician or letter-reader ‘does not know’ what signs have settled
english: Settled medical and documentary judgments are still knowledge in common speech.
Le Blanc’s analogies press Rome’s ‘nescire’ rhetoric as verbal inversion.

title: Popular Roman preaching of ignorance clashes with the Schools’ moral certainty—FINIS Certitudine
english: School usage itself refuses to call fixed moral judgment ‘ignorance.’
Yet popular Roman preaching of not-knowing trains hearers into suspended minds—Le Blanc’s closing charge as Certitudine ends.

title: Roman doctors: three senses of ‘venial’—from cause, event, or nature
english: Roman School usage splits ‘venial’ three ways: by cause, by event, and by the sin’s own nature.
Sins of ignorance or weakness can still be mortal, yet are called venial insofar as something softens guilt and draws nearer to pardon.

title: ‘Venial from the event’: any sin that actually obtains pardon
english: ‘Venial from the event’ means any sin that repentance actually clears and God pardons.
In that loose sense it is not set against mortal sin as such, but against sins that never are forgiven.

title: Proper sense: lighter sins that do not break charity or earn hell
english: In the proper Roman sense, venial sins are lighter faults that do not war with charity or incur hell’s debt.
Mortals are the graver acts that cannot coexist with love of God and make one liable to eternal punishment.

title: Mortal sin: turns from God, kills spiritual life, risks hell if death finds it
english: Roman doctors treat mortal sin as incompatible with charity: it turns the soul from God and kills spiritual life.
If death finds such a sinner unraised by new grace, hell follows—and even the formerly just lose their standing.

title: Venial sin: wounds charity’s fervor without extinguishing grace or earning hell
english: Lighter sins check zeal and love’s fervor without casting out grace or making God an enemy.
They merit temporal penalty only—so death in such a fault does not, of itself, damn.

title: Venials subdivided: of their kind vs. from imperfect performance
english: Roman casuistry splits venials again: some venial by their kind, others only by imperfect performance.
The second class turns on how the act is done, not on a milder species of object.

title: Venial of its kind: disordered object that still does not fight charity
english: A venial-of-its-kind act aims at something disordered that still does not war with charity—idle talk, excess mirth, and the like.
Mortals of their kind (perjury, adultery) openly clash with love of God and neighbor.

title: Venial from imperfect work: could be mortal in kind, softened by how it is done
english: Some acts would be mortal by kind, yet imperfect performance keeps them from being judged as war on charity—hence venial.
Imperfect performance alone can keep an otherwise mortal kind from being judged as war on God’s love.

title: Imperfect-work venials: by surprise (semi-voluntary) or smallness of matter
english: Surprise-venials are sudden, not fully deliberate motions—still culpable if reason could have watched, yet not fully willed.
Small-matter venials are light thefts and the like that do not notably wound neighbor or friendship.

title: Open question: are light sins venial by nature, or only by God’s kindness?
english: Romans agree on lighter vs. graver sins in effect—yet divide on whether light faults are venial by nature or only by God’s milder law.
Some hold eternal damnation for them would clash with justice; others that God could damn them strictly but chooses temporal penalties.

title: Gerson: every offense against God is of itself deadly; veniality is mercy
english: Gerson and allies: every sin could justly earn eternal death; milder imputation is God’s clemency, not the act’s own mildness.
He concludes that any offense against God is of itself deadly and cuts off from glory under justice’s rigor.

title: Gerson’s proofs: any offense outweighs even annihilation
english: Gerson argues any offense against God can justly draw death—even annihilation—because no penalty matches that evil.
Better suffer any punishment than commit the slightest offense against God; else offense could become licit to avoid death.

title: Unremitted offense would exclude forever; pardon is pure liberality
english: Without remission, any offense would forever bar glory and never stop being punished.
Pardon is pure liberality; infinite goods still cannot justify offending God.

title: Corollary: no offense is venial of itself—only relative to mercy
english: Gerson’s first corollary: nothing is venial of itself—only because mercy declines to impute every offense unto death.
Mortal and venial then differ not by essence but by how grace imputes penalty.

title: Thanksgiving owed that venials are not imputed unto death
english: Even venials, for Gerson, deserve thanks that God does not impute them unto death—as with remitted mortals.
He extends the same mercy-logic toward our righteousnesses as filthy rags apart from grace.

title: Fisher of Rochester: agrees veniality is of mercy; difference is grace-flight
english: Fisher grants Luther that ‘venial’ is of mercy, yet marks the real divide: mortal drives out grace and sets one in God’s hatred; venial does not.
Strictly judged, venial may be damnable—but that does not make it mortal in Fisher’s sense.

title: Pius V & Gregory XIII condemn ‘no sin venial by nature’
english: Late-sixteenth-century Belgian denials that any sin is venial by nature were condemned under Pius V and Gregory XIII.
Bellarmine cites the Bull’s article: every sin merits eternal punishment—is rejected as erroneous.

title: Present Roman School: some sins venial by nature—not yet a defined article
english: Today’s Roman consensus: some sins are venial by nature, not merely by mercy.
Le Blanc notes the point is common doctrine, not yet a defined article of faith.

title: Yet venials with mortals in the damned draw everlasting penalty (Thomas)
english: Even while denying venial sin merits hell of itself, the School teaches it is punished eternally in those who die in mortal sin.
Thomas: with mortal sin in the damned, venial draws endless penalty because hell has no remission.

title: Scotus dissents: venial penalty in hell eventually ends
english: Scotus alone here: venial penalty joined to mortal in hell finally ceases; only mortal debts remain forever.
Le Blanc flags him as the noted dissent before stating the common opposite.

title: Common School: venial stain in the damned persists forever—no repentance there
english: Against Scotus, the common line keeps venial punishment perpetual in the damned—no repentance can clear the stain there.
While the stain remains, even light fault keeps them worthy of endless penalty.

title: Still venial by nature: endless hell-penalty for it is only accidental
english: Perpetual hell-penalty for venial sin does not prove it merits hell of itself—the stuckness is accidental to dying in mortal sin.
In the living not under mortal sin, love and contrition can clear venial fault; unpaid debt would still be only temporary...

title: Two intrinsic differences: residual principle of repair; eternal vs temporal debt
english: Mortal sin leaves no inward principle of repair—God must raise as from the dead; venial leaves grace’s life intact.
Even after contrition, unpaid mortal debt can still be eternal; cleared venial guilt leaves only temporal dues—Bellarmine’s line.

title: Dispute: is venial sin against the law, or only beside it?
english: Roman doctors split: Bellarmine’s camp sets venial ‘beside’ the law, mortal ‘against’ it.
Vasquez and others keep both venial and mortal as against God’s law.

title: ‘Beside the law’ softened: material breach, not formal war on charity’s end
english: ‘Beside the law’ advocates still admit a forbidding precept—venial breaks the law materially.
Formally, they say, it is not against the law’s end (charity), because it does not destroy charity—Eustachius’s softening.

title: Another softening: ‘God’s law’ often means only precepts binding under mortal
english: Some reserve ‘God’s law’ for precepts binding under mortal and needful for salvation—hence venial is not ‘simply’ against that law.
They still admit every sin transgresses law broadly, and venial wars with right reason as law’s imprint.

title: Bellarmine: venials are beside the law—imperfect will or imperfect lex
english: Bellarmine: surprise-venials lack full voluntariness, so they are not fully against the law except in a material sense.
Fully willed minor precepts (idle words) are not ‘law’ in rigor, since charity barely measures them.

title: Vasquez’s camp: venial against lesser precepts, not against those needful to charity
english: Vasquez’s side: venial is not against salvation-necessary precepts—yet still against some real, lesser precept.
So ‘beside’ the chief law need not mean ‘not against any precept at all.’

title: Becanus: no venial is properly against the law’s end; all are somehow against law
english: Becanus: venial sin is never properly against the law’s end (charity).
Yet every venial is somehow against the law—perfectly or imperfectly.

title: Becanus: kind- and small-matter venials perfectly against law if deliberate
english: Deliberate kind-venials and small-matter thefts Becanus counts as perfectly against the law.
Sudden indeliberate motions are only imperfectly against precepts like ‘You shall not covet.’

title: Becanus’s close: three ways mortal and venial are not alike against the law—FINIS Prior
english: Becanus closes Prior: mortal alone wars also with the law’s end, and always perfectly, against precepts needful to salvation.
Deliberate venials lack that same threefold alignment—so the Roman map of mortal vs venial ends here before the Protestant Pars Posterior.

title: Protestants: every sin by nature merits eternal death and God’s wrath
english: Reformed consent opens Posterior: every sin, even the lightest in our eyes, deserves everlasting death if God deals by strict right.
The Mosaic curse on imperfect law-keeping sets the frame before any talk of lighter and heavier faults.

title: In the reprobate even the least sins will be punished eternally
english: For the impenitent, even idle words meet everlasting punishment in fact after judgment.
Christian schools agree: past that day only eternal penalty remains.

title: No sin too great for mercy—except the sin against the Holy Spirit
english: Faith and repentance open mercy for any atrocity—save the sin against the Spirit.
That sin means deliberate, malicious casting off of known truth; Hebrews 6 says renewal to repentance is impossible.

title: In the elect all sins are freely remitted through faith in Christ
english: For the elect, even atrocious sins are freely remitted—not repaid by strict penalty.
Grace turns them before death to flee by faith to Christ’s merit and righteousness.

title: Yet sins are not equal—against the Stoic parity of vices
english: Intrinsic desert of death does not make all sins Stoic equals—gravity and penalty have degrees.
Luke’s knowing and ignorant servants mark unequal stripes even where none go free.

title: Second Helvetic Confession: sins unequal; Pelagians and Jovinians condemned
english: Helvetic II—and its Reformed subscribers—deny equal sins and cite harsher judgment than Sodom’s.
Pelagians and Jovinianists who Stoicize vice-parity are expressly damned.

title: Lighter daily sins tolerated in the regenerate without loss of heaven
english: Under the gospel covenant God bears the regenerate’s lighter daily faults without barring heaven.
Idle words, vain thoughts, and flaws in good works can coexist with peace of conscience and hope of salvation.

title: Graver sins cannot stand with a good conscience or title to heaven
english: Grave sins—adultery, idolatry, deliberate murder—cannot share a good conscience or present fitness for heaven.
While they last, peace, assurance, and Spirit-given joy depart; sudden death in them leaves no ground for hope.

title: Scripture: no one is without sin—so some sins coexist with true holiness
english: James, Ecclesiastes, and 1 John prove no believer lives sinless.
Therefore some sins must coexist with true holiness, a good conscience, and the Spirit’s fruits.

title: Scripture equally bars works of the flesh from the kingdom
english: Paul’s catalogs of fleshly works shut their doers out of the kingdom—gospel covenant as well as law.
While someone stays in those crimes, good conscience and lawful assurance of salvation cannot hold.

title: British Dort judgment: daily lighter sins do not shake justification
english: Britain’s Dort judgment: elect justified believers still sin lightly every day.
Those surprise and negligence faults do not shake justification or cut off heavenly inheritance.

title: British explanation: law’s rigor vs gospel fatherly dealing with infirmities
english: Law’s rigor makes every sin deadly; yet God does not always so deal with adopted sons.
Sudden lust-motions, flaws in best works, and unplanned daily slips leave no condemnation in Christ—and do not cast off justification.

title: British third thesis: atrocious falls bring paternal anger and damnable guilt
english: Britain’s third thesis: regenerate saints can plunge into atrocious sins by their own fault.
Then they meet paternal wrath, damnable guilt, and loss of present fitness for heaven.

title: David and Peter prove regenerate can fall—and remain death-liable while impenitent
english: David and Peter show regenerate saints can plunge into grievous sin under God’s permission for humility.
While they rest impenitent they owe damnable guilt, lose present fitness for heaven, and must not pretend safety.

title: Fourth British thesis: the wanderer must return by renewed faith and repentance
english: God’s fixed order: a wandering believer must first return by renewed faith and repentance.
Only then can he be brought to the heavenly goal.

title: Means as sure as the end: elect dying in impenitent vice are not saved
english: Election’s end travels a fixed road of means; the broad path of impenitent vice never reaches heaven.
Paul’s shipwreck word and David/Peter show: elect dying unrepentant in grave sin would not be saved.

title: Fifth thesis: between grave guilt and renewed repentance the sinner stands damnable yet to-be-absolved
english: Between grave guilt and renewed faith-repentance the sinner stands damnable by deserving.
Christ’s merit and God’s purpose mark him for absolution—but not actually absolved until pardon is sought in living faith.

title: Bremen at Dort: grave falls cost good conscience; lighter daily sins do not
english: Bremen’s Dort eleventh thesis matches Britain: grave falls strip conscience, purity, and joy.
Daily lighter slips do not work that loss.

title: Paraeus: fallen faith is sick—habitual only, and does not justify until repentance
english: Paraeus: David-like falls cost heart-cleanness, joy, and conscience; justifying faith then lies sick.
Only habitual faith remains—and God still imputes until repentance restores the act of receiving pardon.

title: Polish Thorn declaration: sins against conscience forfeit justifying grace for a time
english: At Thorn the Poles deny once-justified antinomian security: a relapse that wounds the conscience forfeits justifying grace and the Spirit for that time.hat time.hat time.
Infirmity-slips differ; without special exciting grace unto late repentance such falls leave the sinner damnable in deed.

title: Ames and Crocius: sin that wastes the conscience vs sin that does not
english: Reformed schools (Ames, Crocius) split sins that waste the conscience from those that do not.
Conscience-wasting sin cannot share true piety; infirmity-slips can remain in a godly good conscience.

title: Ursinus/Paraeus: reigning vs non-reigning sin
english: Ursinus (via Paraeus): reigning sin is unresisted and actually death-liable—found in all the unregenerate and in some regenerate falls.
Non-reigning sin is Spirit-resisted; saints keep faith and comfort amid remaining infirmities they hate.

title: Reformed map: two kinds—lighter compatible with holiness; graver death-liable until repentance
english: Reformed doctors thus own two kinds: lighter faults compatible with holiness even at death.
Graver falls, until repentance, make one actually death-liable and unfit for heaven.

title: Reformed reject Rome’s intrinsic venials—yet allow a commodious use of the names
english: Reformed deny Rome’s claim that some sins are by nature non-mortal.
They still allow mortal/venial labels when taken in a careful, commodious sense.

title: Commodious sense: venial by event (pardoned) vs mortal by event (actually damning)
english: First commodious use: ‘venial’ for sins actually pardoned through faith and repentance—even if huge in themselves.
‘Mortal’ then marks sins that in fact damn through unbelief and impenitence—Rome’s ‘from the event.’

title: Venial from cause: infirmity and ignorance obtain mercy more readily than destined malice
english: Second sense: sins of infirmity and ignorance are ‘venial’ as nearer mercy—Paul’s persecuting ignorance.
Destined-malice sins win pardon harder and more often meet eternal death; Rainolds backs the distinction.

title: Gomarus and Piscator: only the sin against the Spirit is mortal as irremissible
english: Some Reformed reserve ‘mortal’ for the irremissible sin against the Spirit—all else ‘venial’ as remissible.
