title: Modern Jesuits unashamed: Costerus, Salazar, de Argento—maternal power over Christ; Mary as Domina Dei
english: Recent Jesuits double down: Costerus—mother heard by authority, not as a servant.
Salazar: lasting maternal/royal power over Christ, used especially when she intercedes.
De Argento: throne above God’s; title Domina Dei—God subjected to her dominion.

title: Dea title in poems and prose—Lipsius, Mendoza, Catharinus, Bembo; Bustis prefer ‘Queen of mercy’
english: Many even give Mary the name Goddess—in verse (Lipsius) and prose (Mendoza, Beroaldus, Catharinus).
Bembo for Leo X speaks of ‘the Goddess’ at Loreto; Bustis allow ‘Goddess of Goddesses’ but prefer Queen of mercy.

title: Alexis de Salo & Tanner: God in the Virgin not only by essence/power/presence or grace but by Identity
english: Alexis de Salo and Tanner: God dwells in Mary beyond essence, power, presence, or grace—by Identity.

title: Marian dominion is real power: she dispenses all grace—Salazar, Lapide, Pelbart as treasurer of divine gifts
english: Marian dominion is real power, not an empty title—she dispenses God’s grace to all.
Salazar: every grace-flow via Mary as moon; Lapide: treasurer of divine graces; Pelbart: no Spirit-gift without her dispensation.

title: Mary as God’s cellarer and neck of the body—Salazar: other Saints’ influx only as moon mediating
english: Bustis: God made Mary His cellarer—nothing reaches us but by her hands.
Alexis: she is the Church’s neck and grace-basin; Osorius: every good hangs on her.
Salazar: other Saints’ help only through Mary as mediating moon.

title: Even temporal goods: Salazar’s householder analogy—Mary holds the keys of worldly expenses
english: Not only spiritual goods: Salazar compares Mary to a trusted wife holding the household keys.
God gives her guardianship of temporal goods—worldly outlays pass through her hands.

title: Some say Mary made and governs the world—Biel, Alanus, Salazar after Bonaventure
english: Some go further: Mary as cause who made, conserves, and governs the world.
Biel and Alanus speak so; Salazar after Bonaventure: by her disposition the world she founded with God perseveres.

title: Bernardinus of Siena: Mary did more for God than God for man—Rivet and Drelincourt collect the sayings
english: Bernardinus of Siena: Mary did more for God than God for humankind—so God is much obliged to us for her sake.
Rivet and Drelincourt gather such sayings; Le Blanc sends the curious reader there.

title: Private only, yet not disapproved: sainted speakers, approved books, pastors fostering popular devotion
english: These sayings are private, not conciliar definitions—yet Rome does not disapprove.
Evidence: the harshest speakers are canonized; books carry episcopal and even papal approbation; pastors foster them in popular devotion.

title: When Protestants object, grave Romans excuse rather than openly damn—Bellarmino, Richelieu, Camus
english: Protestant objections meet excuse, not open damnation, from heavy Roman names.
Bellarmino, Richelieu, and Camus vs Drelincourt illustrate the pattern.

title: Expurgatory Indices leave Marian extremes untouched while cutting Augustine’s anti-temple-to-Saints lines
english: Expurgatory Indices scrub suspects—but leave these Marian extremes untouched.
They even cut Augustine’s lines against temples to Saints/Angels, while Bernardinus, Bembo, Costerus, Catharinus pass.

title: Relics and images deferred; of faith that Saints may be invoked—yet not necessary that each Catholic actually invoke them (Holden)
english: Relics and images matter most for Saint-honor but are reserved for a later dispute.
Of faith: Saints may be licitly invoked—yet not that every Catholic must actually invoke them.
Holden: invocation is useful, not a binding actual duty; some Catholics are saved who never invoked Saints.
Romana closes at LXXVII; next frontier is Pars Secunda (Reformata).

title: Sum of the Roman doctrine: a middle cult between divine majesty and merely civil honor
english: Le Blanc opens Pars Secunda by compressing the Roman account he has already given.
Rome, on that account, assigns angels and canonized people a middle honor.
That honor sits above civic respect for outstanding neighbors and below the worship God's majesty requires.
The lower comparison is with rank, power, and natural gifts, not with anything beyond nature.

title: Roman cult of Saints is analogical, and only loosely called religious or adoration
english: Rome does not put Saint-honor in the same univocal class as worship that belongs to God alone.
The link is analogy, not identity of kind.
Religious and adoration may be used of it only in a looser, less proper sense.
In the stricter use, adoration stays reserved for God.

title: Latria and dulia, with hyperdulia for Mary, though Scripture does not keep the distinction exactly
english: The Schools coined Latria for worship of God and Dulia for honor of holy angels and people.
Dulia is then split: Hyperdulia for the Blessed Virgin, and Dulia in the strict sense for the other Saints.
They admit Scripture itself does not keep that Latria–Dulia split with exactness.

title: Interior acts differ easily from divine worship; exterior signs mostly do not, except sacrifice
english: On Rome's account, inward acts of Saint-honor are easy to tell apart from inner worship of God
outward signs are mostly shared by both religionsionsions.
The stated exception is sacrifice, together with altars, temples, and priests that belong to it.

title: No sacrifice to a creature, yet Masses in Saints' honor that commend the offering by their merits
english: Rome refuses a sacrifice properly so called to any creature.
It still honors saints by offering sacrifice to God in their name.
The Mass does more than give thanks: the saint is invoked, and Christ's body and blood, as they hold it, is commended to God by that saint's merits and prayers.
The secret prayers of Andrew and James are cited as the working formulas.

title: Altars as tombs, yet every altar sanctified to Mary and all Saints; temples as basilicas
english: Rome's doctors will not consecrate an altar to a Saint as an altar, but they will as a tomb.
In practice every altar is sanctified to God and also to the Virgin and all the Saints.
Temples are not built for Saints precisely as temples, yet they are raised and dedicated as sacred houses and basilicas where Saints are ritually honored and invoked.

title: The Roman practice: relics, images, feasts, sodalities, and vows
english: Across the Roman Church, Saints are honored in churches named for them.
The rites include bows and kneeling before relics, statues, and images, with candles, incense, and offerings.
Feast days, named confraternities, and vows made and paid to the Saints belong to the same practice.

title: Invocation is the chief part: Saints as guardians who hear even silent prayers
english: The main Roman act toward the Saints is calling on them, in private and in public.
They are supposed to intercede for the Church at large and for each believer.
They are treated as guardians who see each person's need and hear prayers that are never spoken aloud.

title: Saints invoked as intercessors, yet often with the same formulas used toward God
english: Roman doctors say Saints are asked to obtain goods from God, not to be the authors who give them.
In practice people still ask Saints outright for every bodily and spiritual good.
They use the same prayer-forms as toward God, and explain the difference as a difference of sense.

title: Reformers do not deny all honor to Saints; greater excellence deserves greater honor
english: Rome often says the Reformed refuse the Saints every kind of honor.
Le Blanc answers that they unanimously say the opposite.
Created excellence, as well as divine excellence, is owed its own honor.
Grace and glory outrank civil rank and natural gifts, and the honor should rise with them.

title: Saint-honor differs only in degree from civil honor, but in kind from divine worship
english: However high the respect due to people adorned with saving grace and crowned with glory, the Reformed hold it differs from ordinary civil honor only by degree.
The people compared are those who excel by office, rank, or natural excellence.
From the honor God's majesty requires, the same respect differs in its whole kind.

title: The name may be civil, after Augustine, taken from the heavenly city rather than the earthly
english: What the honor is called matters less to them than what it consists in and how it is shown.
They refuse the bare name religious, because religion properly looks only to God's cult.
They prefer civil, or Augustine's phrase, a cult of fellowship and love.
Civil here is taken from the heavenly city of grace and glory, and it still outranks earthly civic respect in degree.

title: Rambour: religious honor for God alone; civil honor of the heavenly city for Saints and angels
english: Rambour divides honor into religious honor owed to God alone and civil honor given to creatures.
Civil honor of the earthly city covers reverence, love, and fear even toward people outside the faith.
Civil honor of the heavenly city is how the household of faith is treated, including mutual esteem in Romans 12 and Philippians 2.
Saints and angels receive that second civil honor: charity and fellowship, not servitude, by praise, love, imitation, and the stirring of zeal.

title: Voetius: the honor is human and civil; one commonwealth of pilgrims and those in the homeland
english: Voetius denies that honor of holy angels and people is religious cult or servitude; it is human and civil.
Against Bellarmine he notes that the Saints were human and, with the angels, fellow-citizens who share one commonwealth with us.
Bellarmine mixes the city of nature with the city of grace.
Pilgrims and those already home are one people, so honor paid to heavenly citizens is still civil, though higher in degree.

title: Chamier: formally civil even when the cause is supernatural glory
english: Chamier splits civil cult into what it is in itself and what causes it.
A cult can be formally civil even when its cause is supernatural.
Honor of the Saints reigning with Christ is of that sort: not causally civil, because their dignity is supernatural, yet wholly distinct from religious cult, and so formally civil.
He allows the alternative name officiosus, dutiful.

title: Chamier: the honor flows from religion as a commanded act, not as the elicited act of religion
english: Chamier will not call Saint-honor religious; he calls it civil or dutiful.
He still says it flows from religion as a commanded act, not as the act religion itself elicits.
Worship of God is religion, as loving is love; civil cult only comes from that worship, as the Samaritan's care of wounds came from love.
An effect of religion is not religion itself.

title: Drelincourt: religious in the strict sense is God alone; in a wider sense, honor paid for God's sake
english: Drelincourt uses religious in a strict sense for what binds the soul to God and sets the manner of worshiping him.
In that sense only God is worshiped religiously, and Saint-honor is the same kind as honor of living believers, higher only in degree.
In a wider sense, religious covers whatever hangs on religion and is done to honor God.
In that wider sense he allows the honor of blessed spirits and of Christ's mother to be called religious.

title: Reformers commonly reject the Latria–Dulia split, because one cult is properly religious and Scripture mixes the words
english: Reformed doctors generally reject dividing religious cult into Latria and Dulia.
Only the cult proper to God deserves the name religious in the proper and simple sense; creature-honor is religious only improperly.
Scripture also mixes the words: latreia sometimes means human service, and douleia is often kept for God's cult alone.

title: Some Reformed, with Chamier, may reserve latria and dulia as names of different kinds, not degrees
english: Some Reformed writers will still keep Latria for God's cult and Dulia for creature-honor, as a useful distinction.
Chamier allows the Greek words only if they name different kinds, not higher and lower degrees.
Religious cult and civil cult are not synonyms and not analogues of one another.

title: Vossius: the Latria–Dulia split is not scriptural or classical, yet not wholly rejected
english: Vossius says neither Scripture nor the classics observe a Latria for God and a Dulia for creatures, as Valla and Vives also grant.
Taken strictly, douleia fits God more than the Saints, since religious service makes us God's servants; Perezius saw this, and Bellarmine's objection fails.
He still does not condemn the distinction, as a guard against ambiguous names, and because Augustine did not refuse it.
The quarrel with Rome is the thing, not the word: they do not leave God's cult whole, but hand a large part of divine honor to the Saints.

title: Only such cult is lawful toward the blessed as suits an absent creature
english: The next question is what honor the Reformed actually grant the blessed, whether human or angelic.
Their general rule is that nothing may be shown them beyond what fits a creature who is absent, or as good as absent.
There is no mutual commerce with such a creature on which a richer cult could rest.

title: Divine cult is whatever cannot truly suit a creature, even if the worshiper denies he takes the object for God
english: Whatever Scripture counts as divine worship is first stripped away from honor of the blessed.
A cult is divine even if the worshiper does not consciously take its object for the supreme God, the first principle and last end.
It is enough that the act cannot really suit a creature, because it assumes something divine in that creature.
The worshiper's mistaken explanation does not change the nature of the act.

title: A cult is divine which treats its object as present everywhere and able to hear every silent prayer at once
english: Divine cult, on this account, treats its object as watching every worshiper, in every place and time, though unseen.
It also treats that object as hearing countless different prayers at once, including unspoken ones, and as able to help each person in a single moment.
Calling the object only God's friend and minister does not change the act.
Majesty and power of that size belong to God alone, whatever people imagine.

title: Feasts, sacred houses, gifts, oaths, vows, and prayers for grace are as divine as sacrifice
english: Feasts, sacred buildings, dedicated gifts, oaths, vows, and prayers for bodily goods and especially for grace and glory count, for the Reformed, as signs of God's own cult, no less than sacrifice.
Rome itself would not excuse sacrifice to a creature by calling it relative, or offered to God's friend so as to be referred at last to God.
The same plea does not excuse dedicating churches, offering gifts, vowing, swearing, or asking grace and glory of a creature.

title: Sacred houses may not be dedicated to angels or Saints for cult, though ancient memorials of martyrs are not condemned
english: Dedicating a sacred building to angels or to Saints in heaven is held altogether unlawful.
The ban covers not only offering them sacrifice there, but honoring and invoking them with any rites.
The old custom is not condemned when churches kept the martyrs' memory, thanked God for their victories, and offered the Eucharist to God, which honored holy men greatly.
Rivet's note on the Apology for the Blessed Virgin is the reference.

title: Feasts are not consecrated to angels or Saints, though a solemn commemoration, as in the English liturgy, is allowed
english: Feast days may not be consecrated to angels or the blessed, because feasts belong to God's solemn worship.
A set day may still solemnly remember certain Saints, thank God for benefits given to them and through them, and propose their virtues for imitation.
Such days are consecrated to God alone, even while they honor holy men.
The English liturgy, which remembers apostles and other holy men, is the example.

title: Swearing by Saints is as forbidden as sacrificing to them
english: Swearing by the Saints is rejected outright.
An oath by any creature is as forbidden as a sacrifice to that creature, because Scripture condemns both swearing by what is not God and sacrificing to any but God.
A secondary oath, on the ground that divine truth shines in the Saints, has no more excuse than a secondary sacrifice on the ground that God's power and goodness appear in them.

title: Vows belong to the Lord alone, not to Saints as gods by participation or as obtainers of goods
english: Vows, Scripture says, are to be made and paid to the Lord alone.
To vow to Saints as gods by participation, or as those who obtain what we need, is as contrary to true piety as offering them sacrifices under the same title.

title: Praying to Saints in the same forms used to God is treason against the divine majesty
english: Using toward the Saints the same prayer-forms used toward God, and asking them for grace, glory, and any bodily or spiritual good, is treated as an offense against God's majesty.
It does not help to call the Saints not the first authors but only givers and stewards under God.
The same pretext would not excuse sacrificing to them.

title: Many honors lawful toward the living are not lawful toward the spirits of the dead
english: It is not only divine worship that may not be moved over to angels or Saints in heaven.
Many honors that are lawful toward people living with us on earth are, by reason and piety, forbidden toward the spirits of the dead.

title: Bowing and kneeling suit the present, not a Saint in America or China, still less one in heaven
english: Greeting, uncovering the head, and bowing are used toward holy people we actually live with, and only when they are present.
It would be absurd to bow or kneel in France, at home or in church, to honor a holy man traveling in the Americas or in China.
Saints reigning with Christ are as far from us as heaven from earth, so those signs toward them are held contrary to reason.

title: Chamier: absent-capable honors are due; genuflection, greeting, and gifts to the needy are not
english: Chamier holds that honor of the Saints is the same in kind as honor of the living, and differs only by being stronger or weaker.
Degree does not change the species.
Acts that can be paid to people who are absent are due; genuflection, greeting, and bowing, which need presence, are not.
Still less are gifts for the needy, such as clothes, lights, bread, and wine.

title: Asking the living to pray with us does not extend to the dead, with whom we cannot communicate
english: Asking trusted pious people to pray with us and for us belongs to honor among those with whom we have real dealings.
No one addresses, aloud or in the heart, a pious man too far away for even a letter, as if someone in Jerusalem had silently begged the help of Paul's prayers while Paul was in prison at Rome.
For that reason Protestants do not ask the dead in Christ, as they ask the living, to help them before God.
The blessed are far off in glory, and there is no way left to tell them what we feel.

title: To suppose the Saints see all men and hear all thoughts is to give them something divine
english: If the Saints in glory are supposed to see everyone everywhere at once, hear their prayers, know their thoughts, give the help asked, and notice everything done in their honor, something divine has been given them.
The signs of honor in question then cease to be human cult and become divine cult.

title: What remains is pious memory, praise, and imitation of faith, hope, and the other virtues
english: Asked what honor of the Saints is left, Le Blanc answers from the Reformed doctors.
It is frequent pious remembrance, a high estimate, praise when there is occasion, and a careful recall of their virtues and great deeds.
Above all it is following their example, receiving their teaching, and striving to match their hope, faith, love, zeal, courage, patience, and humility.

title: Spanheim: Mary's honor is grateful thought, preaching of her virtues, and commendation of her glory
english: Spanheim's account of the honor due to Mary is also the pattern for other Saints.
First comes honoring remembrance that God, in sheer goodness, made her the mother of the Lord who is Father of all.
Second, preaching the virtues Scripture records in her, as an example.
Third, commending the glory and blessedness she enjoys in heaven.

title: Drelincourt: memory, thanks for gifts given through her, her faith, her example, and her blessedness
english: Drelincourt's honor of the Virgin begins with reverent memory, speech, and delight in her praises.
Next the whole heart praises God for grace and benefits given through her.
Her words are believed, her faith is embraced, and the Spirit's lessons through her are followed.
She is an example of believing and of living, her Christian virtues are imitated, and her blessedness is extolled.

title: Rivet: angels, if present, would be received; being unseen and not everywhere, they are not greeted
english: Rivet treats honor of rational creatures, angels and humans, together.
If angels are present we do not know when or where, unless they appear visibly as they once did.
Some are often near and helpful, but there is no conversation with them, they are not everywhere, and they do not search the heart, so we neither speak to them nor greet them with outward signs.
The patriarchs did greet angels whom they received as men; apart from that, angels are spoken of with honor, and their obedience is magnified for imitation.

title: Rivet: the holy memory of great servants, praise without flattery, and nothing that requires them to hear
english: People illustrious for virtue, above all for piety toward God and service of the Church, have a holy and venerable memory.
They are spoken of reverently, their virtues are recalled, they are proposed for imitation, and they receive due praise.
Any further honor must be such as can be paid to people we do not see and who do not hear us.
That kind is worth more because it cannot be flattery or self-interest.

title: Honor rises with God's gifts; the dead are not served as masters but followed as fellow heirs
english: Rivet has observance rise with the gifts God gave, and praise is proportioned, not flattened.
Servitude properly so called is not given to anyone who does not need our work and cannot be served by it.
The dead Saints are not our masters; we are to share their inheritance and follow their steps.
What they most wanted, by imitating Christ, was that we should imitate them.
Pars Secunda is not closed: thesis XLI takes up the honor of the Virgin in particular.
